notes:
Two of these are about how Docket behaves toward the site it is auditing, not
about what it reports.

**Docket now waits as long as your robots.txt asks it to.** `crawler.py` has
always documented "Never hurt the site being audited" as its first design
constraint, and said that `Crawl-delay` from robots.txt overrides the default.
The function that read that value existed, was correct, and was called by
nothing. Against a site asking for five seconds between requests, Docket was
going at about three pages a second. It now keeps the pace the site asks for,
says so in the progress line, and says so again if the crawl runs out of time.

**A robots.txt with two `User-agent: *` groups is read in full.** CDNs insert a
managed block above the file a site wrote, which leaves many sites with two.
Docket kept the first and discarded the rest — on the site that found this,
one rule of fifty-three, and it would have crawled paths the file plainly
closes.

**A crawl that ran out of time knows what it missed.** Unreached URLs were only
recorded when the page limit was what stopped the crawl. Stopped by the time
limit instead, a five-page look at a 1,555-URL site reported full coverage, no
scope note, and findings claiming things were missing site-wide. Those URLs are
now recorded whatever stopped the crawl — counted once each, and no longer
truncated on one path but not the others.

**And the advice names the setting that actually bound it.** Being told to
raise a page limit that was never reached costs you a second crawl to be handed
back the same sentence. When the time limit is what stopped it, Docket now says
so, and works out from the pace it measured how long a full crawl would take.

**"None of them is named in your robots.txt" — when two of the three were.**
Blocking AI search crawlers deliberately is a policy Docket records rather than
objects to. A file that named two of them by hand and let a wildcard catch the
third was told at CRITICAL that none were named, and asked to re-allow the two
it had just decided to block. The two cases are now reported separately, and
the robots.txt snippet offers only the crawlers actually caught by a wildcard.

**Your acronym is not a second brand.** A site whose logo says "RAE" and whose
og:site_name says "Real Academia Española" was told its brand name appears two
different ways. So would BBC, NHS and MIT. An initialism now counts as the same
name written short.
